stories.headline: Mahindra fires up EV price war with flat ₹8-lakh cut across SUV portfolio under battery-as-a-service
stories.title: Mahindra fires up EV price war with flat ₹8-lakh cut across SUV portfolio under battery-as-a-service
stories.summary: Battery financing is changing how electric SUVs compete for buyers, bringing larger battery packs and longer ranges into lower initial price filters
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: Mahindra & Mahindra on Friday expanded its Battery-as-a-Service (BAAS) financing programme across its Electric Origin SUV lineup, moving a flat ₹8 lakh out of the upfront vehicle price of each model—the largest absolute reduction in advertised entry price among major Indian EV makers using such schemes.
The move drops Mahindra’s electric SUVs, otherwise priced from ₹19.45 lakh to ₹21.90 lakh, into an advertised bracket of ₹11.45 lakh to ₹13.90 lakh before battery financing.
In doing so, Mahindra is pushing 59-79 kWh electric SUVs into the consideration set of buyers who might otherwise begin their search with a ₹12-15 lakh petrol, diesel or CNG vehicle.
That reshuffles an increasingly important battle over advertised prices among EV makers.
Mahindra’s BE 6 SPORTEQ now starts at ₹11.45 lakh under BaaS, while the Tata Curvv.ev starts at ₹12.49 lakh after battery financing moves roughly ₹2.3-4.5 lakh out of the upfront price.
JSW MG Motor India’s Hector Tomahawk EV enters at ₹13.99 lakh under BaaS, representing an upfront shift of about ₹2.64-5.5 lakh depending on the variant.
The significance is less about which EV has the lowest headline price than where these vehicles now appear in a consumer’s shopping journey.
Car buyers typically begin with a budget rather than a powertrain.

A buyer searching below ₹15 lakh can now encounter mid-size electric SUVs offering claimed test-cycle ranges of 521 km on the XEV 9S, 542 km on the XEV 9e and 557 km on the BE 6 SPORTEQ alongside upper variants of smaller petrol and diesel SUVs.
While Mahindra’s headline entry prices apply to the 59-kWh variants, its BaaS programme also extends to the larger 70-kWh and 79-kWh battery packs.
That puts battery capacities once associated with substantially more expensive EVs within the initial price filter of a mass-market SUV shopper.
The lower entry price, however, is not a discount.

stories.headline: China suspends rescue operations near Nepal-Tibet border over fears of another flood
stories.title: China suspends rescue operations near Nepal-Tibet border over fears of another flood
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 28: Chinese authorities have suspended rescue operations near the Nepal-Tibet border after a lake formed by debris from a landslide began filling with water, raising fears that it could burst its banks and trigger another flood, the BBC reported. Officials have been monitoring rising water upstream from Gyirong port, a key land crossing between Nepal and Tibet that was swept away by a torrent of mud and water following Wednesday’s landslide. According to the BBC, hours of heavy rain have increased concerns that the newly formed lake could breach the debris blocking it and cause further flooding in the coming days. Rescuers in the area have reportedly been ordered to halt operations temporarily, citing reports in Chinese state media. More than 550 people have been reported missing on the Tibetan side, including around 260 foreigners. Many of those affected were pilgrims travelling towards Mount Kailash, a major Hindu and Buddhist pilgrimage site in Tibet. The latest disaster has caused heavy casualties on both sides of the border. At least 469 people have died in Nepal, with hundreds still missing, more than 48 hours after flash floods devastated the Himalayan border region. In Tibet, three people have been confirmed dead and more than 550 are missing, although it remains unclear whether some of the figures overlap. The disaster has disrupted an area visited by tens of thousands of tourists and pilgrims every year.

stories.headline: India has 7,500 Himalayan glacial lakes, 200 are high risk amid flood fears
stories.title: India has 7,500 Himalayan glacial lakes, 200 are high risk amid flood fears
stories.summary: Nepal's alarming glacial lake outburst flood serves as a wake-up call for India, which is home to about 200 vulnerable glacial lakes in the Himalayas. The GLOF incident in Sikkim resulted in severe damage, highlighting the urgency of proactive measures. In response, the Indian government has launched a National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme focused on thorough assessments, continuous monitoring, effective early warnings, and raising awareness within local communities.

stories.headline: The warning Kishtwar already documents
stories.title: The warning Kishtwar already documents
stories.summary: Sometime on a Wednesday morning this month, a wall of water came down the Bhotekoshi on the Nepal-China border. It began with a magnitude 4.4 tremor about a hundred kilometres north of Kathmandu. Minutes later, researchers believe, an ice avalanche broke loose in the Lhende Khola and pushed a surge into Rasuwa and Nuwakot. By the time the water reached the plains it had taken out hydropower stations and buried villages, and a mudslide in Gyirong county on the Tibetan side added to the count. Officials in both countries have confirmed at least 98 dead ( at the time of writing this column), with hundreds missing. Early Indian reports suggested more than a hundred Indian nationals were on the Kailash pilgrim route that runs through the same valley. The detail that should trouble Indian planners is not the death toll. It is that the same stretch of river did this in July 2025, when a supraglacial lake drained upstream in Tibet and killed nine people. Fourteen months, twice. The mountain gave the same warning on two occasions, and on both it was filed as an isolated tragedy rather than read as a pattern. I have been thinking about that pattern because of a document produced by the District Disaster Management Authority in Kishtwar: its Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Risk Management Plan for 2024-25. It is a serious piece of work by the district’s own officials, and it is unusually candid. It is also, read closely, an inventory of everything that has not yet been built. Kishtwar is known to most Indians for its mountain scenery and, increasingly, for its dams. Very few know that it holds the largest concentration of glacial lakes anywhere in Jammu and Kashmir. By the DDMA’s own assessment, the district contains 197 glacial lakes, 36.08 per cent of every glacial lake in the Union Territory, spread over roughly 392 hectares in the upper Chenab basin. Most are small. About 91 per cent are under five hectares. The risk sits with the exceptions, the ones still growing as the glaciers behind them retreat. The plan singles out four. Mundiksar and Hangu are classified High Risk. An unnamed lake near 33.94°N, 76.02°E, and Patla Pani are classified Moderate Risk. These are not activist estimates. They were compiled by the district administration with the UT’s disaster management department and cross-checked against the seventeen-parameter scoring framework the Central Water Commission finalised in October 2024, which weighs lake size, dam type, seismic exposure, freeboard and distance to habitation. Mundiksar is the one worth sitting with. At about 4,071 metres and 39.44 hectares, it has expanded visibly over four decades as its parent glacier has pulled back, a change the plan’s own satellite comparisons from 1980 to 2020 document in detail. It is on the National Disaster Management Authority’s lake registry. And yet, by the plan’s own expedition record, current as of November 2024, no field survey report had been received for any of Kishtwar’s three most concerning lakes. Mundiksar, Hangu and the unnamed lake were all assigned to the Central University of Jammu for physical assessment. All three appear in the district’s own table as “Not Received”. Two lakes elsewhere in the valley, Sheshnag and Sona Sar, had their reports filed on schedule. Kishtwar’s had not. This is not a failure of scientists. It is a resourcing gap, and the plan says so plainly: the district “lacks access to advanced technology and equipment” and depends on national institutions for timely data. The scale of that gap is easy to state. Across all Himalayan river basins in India, the CWC’s satellite programme actively tracks 902 glacial lakes and water bodies. Of those, 15 glacial lakes and 16 water bodies fall within the whole of Jammu and Kashmir. One district holds 197. On the UT’s own 24-lake priority watchlist, Kishtwar contributes three, against nine for Ganderbal and eight for Anantnag. Its share of formal study attention has not caught up with its share of the hazard. What makes this a national question rather than a district one is what sits downstream. Kishtwar is becoming one of India’s most important hydropower corridors, home to the Pakal Dul, Kiru, Kwar and Dangduru projects under Chenab Valley Power Projects Limited. The DDMA’s plan states directly that these face real exposure to GLOF-driven surges, sediment loads and structural damage. India has committed enormous public capital to harnessing the Chenab. The same report that documents the risk to that investment is the one whose surveys on the critical lakes remain incomplete. Add one more fact and the calculus changes again. Kishtwar sits in Seismic Zone IV. A flood here would not require an unusual monsoon. A moderate earthquake could destabilise an already weakened moraine dam on its own, which is precisely the sequence that played out in Nepal this month. Two independent hazards capable of triggering each other are harder to predict and far more expensive to manage than either alone. The plan does not stop at description, to its credit. It calls for automated real-time sensors on high-risk lakes, an early warning system built with the India Meteorological Department, controlled drainage and reinforcement of unstable moraine dams, and evacuation mapping done before rather than after an event. It points to Section 10.3.6 of the NDMA’s 2020 GLOF guidelines, which allows District Planning and Development Council funds to be earmarked for exactly this work. Every one of these is sound. Not one is self-executing. A plan that recommends a drainage tunnel is not a drainage tunnel, and a committee that meets twice a year is not a sensor transmitting live data from 4,000 metres. The plan names five tehsils as most exposed: Padder, Machail, Dachhan, Marwah and Warwan. Marwah and Warwan it calls “Shadow Areas”, the district’s own term for places so remote that emergency response is stretched thin in ordinary times, let alone during a flood that arrives with minutes of notice. I did not expect to find my own family’s valley on that list. Dachhan is on it, in the district’s own words, and I cannot write around that. It is also the reason I think the rest of the country should read this document rather than wait for it to be quoted in a post-disaster inquiry. Kishtwar has what Rasuwa did not: a report that already names the lakes, the villages and the projects at risk. Disasters are rarely sudden. They begin years earlier, in surveys marked “Not Received”, while the lakes keep expanding on a schedule of their own. Lokesh Dhar is a public policy researcher and consultant.

stories.headline: Nepal GLOF tragedy puts spotlight on Kashmir’s lagging preparedness
stories.title: Nepal GLOF tragedy puts spotlight on Kashmir’s lagging preparedness
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 28: The recent glacial lake outburst flood in Nepal has sharpened focus on vulnerabilities at home. There is a chasm in J&K, between the on-ground preparedness here, compared with other Himalayan states. Five glacial lakes in the Kashmir Himalayas, the Bramsar, Chirsar, Nundkol, Gangabal and Bhagsar, have been classified as having “very high susceptibility” to Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). This was revealed by a study by Department of Geoinformatics, University of Kashmir, published in the Journal of Glaciology. The lakes, as per the study, threaten roughly 2704 buildings, about 15 major bridges, stretches of road and one hydropower plant in Ganderbal, Shopian, and Kulgam districts. Associate Professor at Department of Geoinfomatics, University of Kashmir, Irfan Rashid, said the lakes are not "unstable" at present, but nevertheless "risky". "In a few years, the lakes like Gangabal may be a risk. Gangabal has Harmukh glacier upstream, and it is on a steep slope. In view of disaster like that of Nepal, we must take into account such factors as well," he said. In addition, Rashid said, glacial-lake volume assessment could help in improving data that Government must take into consideration. "Our urban planning and disaster mitigation policies need to take into account the environment and geological research carried out by academia here," he said. Rashid said that Chirsar and Bramsar, two glacial lakes in Kulgam district have an ice-contacts - lakes have formed at the terminal point of the glacier. Among lakes in Kashmir, these have the highest susceptibility to GLOF, he said. Earlier this year, a reply to a starred question in the Legislative Assembly had the government acknowledging the findings. The government outlined a roadmap that included continuous remote-sensing and field monitoring, installation of early-warning systems, bathymetric surveys planned for 2026, development of ecozonation plans, and integration of GLOF scenarios into district disaster plans. The work on mountain-specific early-warning prototypes that combine satellite data, field observations and real-time sensors is already underway at University of Kashmir. However, these measures have largely remained on paper only. Many Himalyan states have made progress. Sikkim now has operational water-level sensors, automatic weather stations and India’s first dedicated GLOF early-warning system. This followed the 2023 South Lhonak disaster. Himachal Pradesh has a C-DAC prototype which has been tested at Sissu and is being scaled up. J&K has no real-time monitoring hardware or functional early-warning network. Bathymetric surveys needed for accurate flood modelling are a far call. Dr Rashid said risk mitigation in Himalayas will require study of thousands of lakes. This, he said, is a serious and long-term exercise. The national GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme has initially prioritised Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh. Kashmir and Ladakh were added later. While the scientific baseline in Kashmir has a solid scientific strength, the absence of installed sensors, operational alerts and completed field assessments leaves it lagging. This is crucial as climate-driven glacial risks are rising across the Himalayan range.

stories.headline: Defence Ministry eases export rules to boost defence exports
stories.title: Defence Ministry eases export rules to boost defence exports
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 28: The Ministry of Defence has introduced a series of reforms to simplify procedures for defence exports and make it easier for Indian manufacturers to access international markets. The reforms, undertaken by the Department of Defence Production under the guidance of Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, aim to reduce procedural requirements while ensuring that national security safeguards remain in place. Under the revised Defence Export Standard Operating Procedure (SOP), stakeholder consultation will no longer be required for exports of non-lethal defence items to most destinations, except sensitive countries. The requirement has also been removed for exports of all items for international tenders and exhibitions, allowing Indian companies to pursue overseas opportunities more quickly. The Ministry has also substantially revised the Open General Export Licence (OGEL) framework. The OGEL is a standing export authorisation that allows eligible companies to undertake multiple consignments of specified defence items without obtaining a separate licence for each shipment. Three existing OGEL SOPs covering major platforms and equipment, parts and components, and intra-company transfer of technology have been merged into a single unified SOP. The validity of OGEL has also been increased from two to three years, reducing the need for frequent renewals. The countries covered under OGEL have been expanded from 41 to all countries, barring specified sensitive or restricted nations and countries facing UN Security Council sanctions or arms embargoes. A new provision will also facilitate Indian companies that have long-term contracts with foreign original equipment manufacturers. In eligible cases, OGEL validity can be aligned with the duration of the underlying contract, subject to prescribed conditions. The range of items eligible for OGEL has also been expanded. The revised framework permits civil-end-use exports of specified parts and components of small-calibre arms and protective equipment. The government said the reforms would particularly benefit Indian defence manufacturers, including MSMEs, by reducing repetitive approvals and enabling them to respond faster to international tenders and exhibitions. The government said the changes are aimed at further strengthening India’s position as a reliable and competitive global defence manufacturing and export partner, in line with the objectives of Make in India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat.

opening: New Delhi, Aug 28: The Ministry of Defence has introduced a series of reforms to simplify procedures for defence exports and make it easier for Indian manufacturers to access international markets.

The reforms, undertaken by the Department of Defence Production under the guidance of Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, aim to reduce procedural requirements while ensuring that national security safeguards remain in place.
body: Under the revised Defence Export Standard Operating Procedure (SOP), stakeholder consultation will no longer be required for exports of non-lethal defence items to most destinations, except sensitive countries.
The requirement has also been removed for exports of all items for international tenders and exhibitions, allowing Indian companies to pursue overseas opportunities more quickly.
The Ministry has also substantially revised the Open General Export Licence (OGEL) framework.
The OGEL is a standing export authorisation that allows eligible companies to undertake multiple consignments of specified defence items without obtaining a separate licence for each shipment.
Three existing OGEL SOPs covering major platforms and equipment, parts and components, and intra-company transfer of technology have been merged into a single unified SOP.
The validity of OGEL has also been increased from two to three years, reducing the need for frequent renewals.
The countries covered under OGEL have been expanded from 41 to all countries, barring specified sensitive or restricted nations and countries facing UN Security Council sanctions or arms embargoes.
A new provision will also facilitate Indian companies that have long-term contracts with foreign original equipment manufacturers.
In eligible cases, OGEL validity can be aligned with the duration of the underlying contract, subject to prescribed conditions.
The range of items eligible for OGEL has also been expanded.
The revised framework permits civil-end-use exports of specified parts and components of small-calibre arms and protective equipment.

The government said the reforms would particularly benefit Indian defence manufacturers, including MSMEs, by reducing repetitive approvals and enabling them to respond faster to international tenders and exhibitions.

The government said the changes are aimed at further strengthening India’s position as a reliable and competitive global defence manufacturing and export partner, in line with the objectives of Make in India and Aatmanirbhar Bharat.

stories.headline: Lawyers must re-enter political mainstream
stories.title: Lawyers must re-enter political mainstream
stories.summary: India’s democratic journey has always been closely intertwined with the legal profession. From the struggle for independence to the making of the Constitution and the establishment of parliamentary democracy, lawyers played an extraordinary role in shaping the nation. The freedom movement was not merely a political struggle; it was also a struggle for civil liberties, equality, dignity and the rule of law. Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Dr. Rajendra Prasad and countless other lawyers stepped beyond their courtrooms to stand with the people and lead the country towards freedom. The composition of the first Parliament of independent India reflected this remarkable tradition. Around 70 lawyers were members of the first Lok Sabha. Their presence was not accidental. They understood that political freedom would have little meaning unless it was translated into constitutional governance, social justice, economic opportunity and protection of individual rights. Their legal training enabled them to participate meaningfully in framing laws, scrutinising executive action and building the institutional architecture of the Republic. It is worth asking why this tradition has weakened over the years. Lawyers continue to occupy a position of considerable respect in courts and public discourse, and many distinguished members of the profession continue to serve in Parliament and State legislatures. Yet, in relative terms, the participation of lawyers in electoral politics and public life has declined. This should concern everyone committed to the health of Indian democracy. When lawyers withdraw from public life, politics loses an important source of constitutional knowledge, institutional experience and principled accountability. The courtroom and the political arena are different, but they are not disconnected. A lawyer appearing before a constitutional court may argue about fundamental rights, federalism, separation of powers or administrative accountability. A legislator must confront these very principles while making laws and scrutinising government. Lawyers understand how an apparently simple administrative decision can affect the liberty, livelihood, property or dignity of an ordinary citizen. This experience can make an important contribution to public policy. Lawyers are also professionally trained to question power. Legal practice requires examining facts, testing evidence, identifying contradictions and demanding reasons for the exercise of authority. In a democracy, these qualities are indispensable. Political power must remain accountable; legislation must be carefully scrutinised; executive authority must remain within constitutional limits; and institutions must function according to law. Lawyers are therefore naturally equipped to ask a fundamental democratic question: Is this exercise of power lawful, fair and constitutionally justified? At the same time, legal training alone does not make someone a good politician or administrator. Politics requires empathy, patience, social understanding, organisational ability, communication, political judgment and moral courage. A lawyer entering politics must understand the lives of people beyond the courtroom—the farmer facing agrarian distress, the worker seeking employment, the student struggling for opportunity, the displaced family seeking rehabilitation and the young person searching for a secure future. That is precisely why more lawyers should enter public life. Their purpose should not be to create a separate class of legal politicians, but to bring constitutional consciousness into the political process. They can help bridge the gap between constitutional promises and everyday realities. They can explain complex questions of law and policy in language ordinary citizens understand, challenge misinformation and insist that political programmes remain consistent with constitutional values. Justice, after all, is not confined to courtrooms. Poverty, unemployment, discrimination, displacement, custodial violence, unequal access to education and healthcare, environmental degradation and denial of basic services are also questions of justice. Courts can provide remedies in individual cases, but many structural problems require legislative and political solutions. Laws have to be enacted, budgets allocated, institutions strengthened and policies implemented. Lawyers who understand both the law and the lived experience of citizens can therefore make a significant contribution to translating constitutional ideals into effective governance. This responsibility becomes even more important as India’s young population becomes increasingly politically conscious. Gen Z is not merely an audience of politics; it is increasingly becoming a participant in it. Young Indians are entering public debate with new expectations of transparency, accountability, employment, quality education and dignity. They are also confronting questions relating to climate change, technology, artificial intelligence, privacy, data protection, surveillance and freedom of expression in the digital age. The legal fraternity must engage with this generation—not merely as teachers, but as listeners and partners. Gen Z is bringing new forms of political participation and communication. Lawyers must understand these changes and help ensure that technological and social transformation takes place within the framework of constitutional rights and human dignity. Artificial intelligence and digital technologies, for example, raise profound questions about privacy, employment, intellectual property, discrimination, surveillance and accountability. Social media has transformed political communication while creating new challenges involving misinformation and freedom of expression. These are not distant legal questions. They will directly influence the future of Indian democracy. Lawyers with a sound understanding of constitutional principles have an important role in ensuring that technological progress does not come at the cost of fundamental freedoms. Lawyers can also bring greater seriousness and evidence-based reasoning to political debate. Their professional experience encourages them to distinguish fact from allegation and argument from evidence. But legal expertise must never become a means of hiding moral responsibility behind technicalities. Constitutionalism is not merely about procedures and institutional boundaries. At its heart are human dignity, liberty, equality and justice. Political parties and the Bar also have responsibilities. Political parties should encourage lawyers of integrity, competence and public commitment to enter electoral politics and legislative institutions. Opportunities should be created for younger members of the Bar to participate in policy discussions, legislative research and public affairs. Bar associations can promote constitutional literacy, public-policy debates, legal aid and civic engagement. Entering public life does not necessarily mean contesting an election. Lawyers can contribute as legislators, political organisers, policy advisers, researchers, local representatives, civil-society leaders and educators. What matters is a willingness to accept public responsibility and use professional knowledge in the larger service of society. The legal profession has historically understood that law is ultimately about people. The courtroom remains an essential institution of justice, but it cannot be the only arena in which lawyers serve the nation. Democracy also needs committed citizens in legislatures, political organisations, public institutions and communities. I therefore urge more and more lawyers to enter the polity of India. The country needs their constitutional understanding, their ability to question authority, their commitment to institutions and their experience of defending the rights of citizens. At a time when democratic institutions face new challenges and a new generation is seeking a greater voice in India’s future, the legal fraternity cannot remain a silent spectator. The lawyers who participated in India’s freedom movement understood that their professional knowledge carried a national responsibility. Those who helped build the Republic understood that independence had to be secured through constitutional democracy. The challenge before our generation is to carry that legacy forward. India’s democracy needs lawyers not only in courtrooms, but also in Parliament, State legislatures, political organisations and public life. The time has come for the legal fraternity to reclaim its historic role in shaping the political, constitutional and democratic future of the nation. Author is a political analyst and Senior Advocate in Supreme Court of India.

stories.headline: Resignation will come, accountability first: Ruhullah writes to NC Chief
stories.title: Resignation will come, accountability first: Ruhullah writes to NC Chief
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 28: Srinagar MP and National Conference leader Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi has escalated his differences with party president Dr Farooq Abdullah, saying he would resign but insisting that “accountability must come first”. In a detailed letter to Abdullah dated August 28, Ruhullah questioned the National Conference’s position on the restoration of Article 370 and argued that statehood cannot be treated as a substitute for the constitutional protections removed in August 2019. Ruhullah said he was responding to recent remarks by Abdullah, including, “How long will you be a slave? You have to stand on your feet sometimes. When will you stand?” He also referred to Abdullah’s reported remark, “You want 370, but you beg from Delhi.” Addressing Abdullah as “Doctor Sahab”, Ruhullah said the remarks reflected a frustration felt by many people in Jammu and Kashmir. “I must confess, those words resonated deeply with me. They captured a frustration many of us in Jammu-Kashmir feel: that even while asking for what is rightfully ours, we are expected to assume a posture of supplication before the BJP,” he wrote. Ruhullah questioned the party’s current emphasis on restoration of statehood instead of Article 370 and 35A. He said statehood was a right recognised by the Supreme Court and had also been promised by the BJP in its 2024 Assembly election manifesto. Accepting statehood as the limit of the party’s demands, he argued, would amount to “legitimising and normalising the constitutional assault of August 2019”. Ruhullah also questioned why the NC included restoration of Articles 370 and 35A in its 2024 election manifesto if the party believed the commitments could not be fulfilled. “Were we making promises we knew we could not keep or perhaps never truly intended to keep?” he asked. He said he did not want to be part of what he described as a political “lie”, alleging that he had faced a “coordinated campaign of rebuke” within the party over his position. Defending his position, Ruhullah said Article 370 represented the struggle for the dignity, constitutional guarantees and liberties of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. He also highlighted unemployment, land and resources, religious rights, language, traditions and environmental degradation as issues requiring political attention. “Nearly 65% of Jammu and Kashmir's population is young, and their future is increasingly uncertain, with no jobs and opportunities. Our land is up for grabs. Our resources benefit everybody but us,” he wrote. He said elected representatives should seek stronger constitutional safeguards rather than limit their aspirations to what the BJP government was willing to concede. Ruhullah also referred to Abdullah’s political record, recalling that he was chief minister when the erstwhile Jammu and Kashmir Assembly passed the Autonomy Resolution. “I do not ask these questions out of disrespect. I ask them because I remember that you were the Chief Minister of the very Assembly that passed the Autonomy Resolution. That, too, must have required courage,” he wrote. “What has changed, the aspirations of our people, or the JKNC's willingness to stand up for them?” he asked. On the question of his resignation, Ruhullah said he would await Abdullah’s response to the issues raised in his letter. “There are many more questions. But for now, I will await your response to these and so will the people of Jammu-Kashmir, who have a right to know what the JKNC truly stands for,” he wrote. “Rest assured, the resignation will come. It would have come even without you asking but before that must come accountability.” The letter marks a further escalation in Ruhullah’s differences with the NC leadership over Article 370, statehood and the party’s political position on the constitutional changes of August 2019.

stories.headline: Srinagar sizzles at 33.5°C
stories.title: Srinagar sizzles at 33.5°C
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 28: Jammu and Kashmir remained hot and humid Friday, with Srinagar recording 33.5 degrees Celsius, its highest temperature in August 2026 so far. The brief heat spell is expected to peak Saturday, with temperatures likely to rise slightly before easing from August 31, the Meteorological Centre said. Srinagar's maximum temperature rose from 32.9 degrees Celsius Thursday to 33.5 degrees Celsius Friday. Kupwara also recorded 33.5 degrees Celsius, up from 33.3 degrees Celsius. Qazigund recorded 32.6 degrees Celsius, Kokernag 31 degrees Celsius, Pahalgam 27.3 degrees Celsius and Gulmarg 23.8 degrees Celsius. In the Jammu region, Jammu city recorded 34.6 degrees Celsius, Katra 32.5 degrees Celsius, Banihal 30.4 degrees Celsius, Bhaderwah 30.6 degrees Celsius, and Batote 28.1 degrees Celsius. Minimum temperatures in Kashmir also remained generally high and above normal, while those in the Jammu region mainly stayed close to normal. The weather office forecast light to moderate rain and thundershowers at scattered to many places on August 31. Brief spells of intense rain may occur during the early morning and afternoon. Hot and humid conditions are likely to continue into the first week of September, even as temperatures gradually decline. Isolated rain or thundershowers are expected on September 1 and 2. Similar conditions are forecast from September 3 to 5, with rainfall activity largely confined to isolated areas. The MeT office warned that intense localized showers could trigger flash floods, mudslides and landslides in vulnerable areas. August has largely remained dry in the Valley. Temperatures generally hovered around 30-32 degrees Celsius in the plains. Rainfall was mostly limited to isolated showers, including some intense spells in higher reaches. The current heat spell is expected to be brief, with temperatures easing from August 31. Srinagar had recorded 35.3 degrees Celsius on June 29 and 35.5 degrees Celsius on June 30-the highest for the month. Temperatures reached 35 degrees Celsius on July 17 and 35.9 degrees Celsius on July 18, the highest of the summer so far.
